newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian chamber agrees anti-NATO debate.
newsitem.headline: Russian chamber agrees anti-NATO debate.

text.p: Russian deputies gave President Boris Yeltsin an extra reason to be tough with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki by voting on Wednesday to debate a resolution declaring that Moscow would never join NATO.

The debate itself, likely to give voice to bitter hostility to the Western military alliance on all sides of the chamber, will take place on Thursday, coinciding with the first day of the U.S.-Russian summit in the Finnish capital.

In a separate move, the State Duma lower house, which is dominated by the communist opposition, also decided to ask Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to explain a radical government shake-up that has put reformers in key cabinet positions.
Chernomyrdin's office said on Wednesday that he would chair the first meeting of his new cabinet on Thursday morning.

The conservative Duma decided to consider the non-binding resolution "On the inadmissibility of Russia's joining NATO" just a day before Yeltsin was due to leave for a summit likely to be dominated by a search for compromise over NATO expansion.
The resolution appeared to be a purely symbolic gesture since neither NATO nor the Kremlin have raised the possibility of Russia becoming part of the Western alliance.
But it reflected the deep unease still felt among the Russian leadership and public about relations with NATO.

"Moscow sacrificed many things for the sake of friendship with Washington over the last five years," the liberal newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda said, referring to the period after the collapse of the Soviet Union in late 1991. "But many of Washington's promises have never been put into effect."

Bitter opposition to NATO's plans to grant full membership to some eastern and central European countries is probably the only major issue on which the Kremlin leader and his communist and nationalist opponents are united.

"Russia's (negative) approach to NATO expansion will not change regardless of any summits, bilateral meetings and negotiations," Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters in Helsinki.
But NATO has made clear it will not drop its expansion plans to please Moscow and the Kremlin has been focusing on working out a legally binding deal to guarantee its security interests.

Moscow wants such a deal to include a NATO promise not to deploy its troops or nuclear arms on the territory of new members and a pledge never to admit former Soviet republics, including the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
The parliamentary resolution also reflected fears among deputies, most of whom are hostile to Yeltsin, that the president may make a bold move to settle relations with NATO.

Yeltsin, back at the helm after long illness, has proved over the past week that he is still capable of decisive steps, with a radical cabinet reshuffle that put youthful liberals like Anatoly Chubais in charge of economic policy.
Yeltsin's changes also included scrapping several ministries, including the Industry Ministry and the Defence Industry Ministry, to make government more efficient.
"Under the disguise of reorganising the government they are destroying industry, agriculture and other sectors," Interfax news agency quoted nationalist deputy Sergei Baburin as saying.
The Duma, which loathes Chubais for his pro-market views and role in Yeltsin's re-election campaign last year, invited Chernomyrdin to the chamber on Friday to explain the changes.
Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov later said Chernomyrdin had agreed to come.
Despite its criticism of the changes, the Duma has no say in the reshuffle because it only has the right to reject appointments if the prime minister himself has been changed.
